items.questionAndWhy: How do people acquire hidden regularities from repeated experience, and do common learning tasks measure the same process?
items.whatTheyDid: Conway and colleagues synthesized research on embedded-pattern, artificial-grammar and serial-reaction-time tasks, separating computational goals, cognitive operations and neural implementation.
items.whatTheyFound: The review identifies prediction-based learning and chunk formation as distinct but overlapping processes, supported by basal-ganglia and medial-temporal systems. Task design, input and learner characteristics can shift their relative contributions. This is a conceptual synthesis, not a new pooled effect estimate.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX learning experiments could separately measure prediction of the next event and recognition of familiar sequences. Success on one statistical-learning task should not be treated as proof of a single general learning mechanism.
items.streamTitle: Statistical learning relies on multiple interacting processes
items.streamSummary: A neuroscience review distinguishes predictive learning from chunking and maps both onto multiple neural systems; a single task cannot uniquely identify the mechanism.
items.attribution: Conway, Janacsek, Buffington et al. — Nature Reviews Neuroscience (review; November 25, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: After a major societal shock, do groups return to their previous behavior at different rates, or do persistent gaps reflect the initial disruption?
items.whatTheyDid: Cabrera and colleagues analyzed more than 170 million aggregated, anonymized Meta-Facebook location records in Argentina, Chile and Colombia from April 2020 through May 2022, comparing mobility against prepandemic baselines.
items.whatTheyFound: Mobility in the densest urban areas remained approximately 25–50% below baseline two years after the initial shock. Affluent areas experienced larger initial declines; estimated recovery slopes were similar across groups. Platform selection and aggregate data limit inference about individual motives or remote work.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX crisis-behavior models can distinguish the size of an initial disruption from the subsequent adaptation rate. Aggregate mobility cannot determine whether individuals changed behavior because of beliefs, preferences or constraints.
items.streamTitle: Initial mobility disruptions accounted for persistent differences in recovery
items.streamSummary: Three-country observational mobility analysis links persistent group differences primarily to initial disruption rather than different modeled recovery rates.
items.attribution: Cabrera, González-Leonardo and Rowe — Nature Communications (observational mobility study; November 26, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: How are disputed claims about EU accession documented across Ukraine, Moldova and Georgia, and what can investigators establish about their origins?
items.whatTheyDid: Baker and Hickey synthesized fact-checks and interviews with journalists and a Moldovan official in a report republished by EU NEIGHBOURS east on November 26.
items.whatTheyFound: Interviewees described recurring claims about sovereignty and economic consequences across platforms, but noted that domestic and foreign sources cannot always be distinguished. The article presents documented examples and attributed interpretations, not a systematic measure of reach or effects.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX defensive information analysis can maintain separate records for factual verification, source attribution and measured audience exposure. The reported narratives do not establish an effect on public opinion or accession decisions.
items.streamTitle: EU enlargement reporting distinguishes recurring narratives from uncertain attribution
items.streamSummary: Reporting on contested EU accession narratives highlights attribution uncertainty and the distinction between documented content and measured audience effects.
items.attribution: Noel Baker and Emma Hickey — The Journal / EU NEIGHBOURS east (journalistic synthesis; November 26, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: Does supplying an appropriate theory improve an AI solver more than supplying examples of equal length, and can models induce that theory independently?
items.whatTheyDid: Gao and Bi tested length-matched context conditions on probability problems and introduced unpublished mathematical rules in custom problem families to separate induction from recall.
items.whatTheyFound: For Qwen3-14B, providing the relevant theory increased first-attempt success from 37% to 83%; median tokens for correct answers fell from 10.2k to 6.3k. Gains diminished with larger budgets and stronger solvers. Induced theories recovered 60%, 48% and almost none of the available gain in three custom families.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX can compare theory-guided research assistants against example-only baselines under equal budgets. Better mathematical task performance does not establish that supplied behavioral theories are true or that AI can discover valid causal explanations.
items.streamTitle: Explicit mathematical theory improved bounded AI problem solving
items.streamSummary: Explicit theory improved mathematical benchmark performance and efficiency, but AI-generated theory was incomplete and results varied across problem families.

items.questionAndWhy: Can researchers improve how AI assistants construct and retrieve memory by locating recurring failures rather than editing prompts in isolation?
items.whatTheyDid: Xu and colleagues developed HoMe, which uses session-level memory versions and execution traces to propose and screen changes to an open-source memory system. They evaluated it on LongMemEval-S and BEAM.
items.whatTheyFound: After a full initial evaluation, six formal candidate evaluations per benchmark produced improved task performance and lower query-time token use relative to the initial harness. Results concern one memory system and two benchmarks; independent generalization was not established.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX research workflows could version memory artifacts and trace failures to their originating sessions before changing retrieval or summarization logic. Evaluate changes on untouched project histories, rather than equating fewer tokens with better evidence retention.
items.streamTitle: Versioned memory traces supported optimization of long-running assistants
items.streamSummary: HoMe used versioned memory and failure traces to improve a tested assistant memory harness on two benchmarks while reducing query-time token use.
items.attribution: Xu, Yu, Liu et al. — arXiv preprint (November 25, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: Can a behavioral assessment report one ability dimension while accounting for other dimensions that affect count-based item responses?
items.whatTheyDid: Sabel, Holling and Doebler derived projection formulas for multidimensional count-data item-response models, estimated dispersion numerically, and evaluated the approach using cognitive-assessment items and simulations.
items.whatTheyFound: Compared with fitting an ordinary one-dimensional model to multidimensional data, projection improved estimation error, rank correlation and confidence-interval coverage. It did not improve bias, nor outperform the full multidimensional model on every metric.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX assessment designers could compare projected and full multidimensional models when test scores count correct responses or other events. Do not assume a convenient single score measures a pure psychological construct; validate it against independent criteria.
items.streamTitle: Projected item-response models improved selected ability-measurement metrics
items.streamSummary: A psychometric preprint reports better selected estimation metrics when projecting multidimensional count responses onto one dimension, with no bias improvement.
items.attribution: Sabel, Holling and Doebler — arXiv preprint (November 25, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: How can analysts estimate whether collecting additional evidence is worth its cost when every possible observation requires a costly decision optimization?
items.whatTheyDid: Friedli, Papaioannou and Straub compared control variates, stratified sampling and importance sampling, including combinations, using an analytical reference problem and two engineering reliability cases.
items.whatTheyFound: The authors linked two value-of-information formulations through a control variate. Suitable combinations improved estimation efficiency across the cases, although relative method performance depended on problem characteristics. No behavioral decision problem was tested.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX could test these estimators when comparing the expected decision benefit of additional survey measurements or model-validation data. Transfer is hypothetical and depends on explicit utilities, uncertainty distributions and credible observation models.
items.streamTitle: Variance reduction made value-of-information estimation more efficient
items.streamSummary: A computational preprint combines variance-reduction techniques to estimate the expected value of evidence more efficiently; behavioral applications remain untested.
items.attribution: Friedli, Papaioannou and Straub — arXiv preprint (November 25, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: How can researchers study brain responses to changing visual events using many standardized naturalistic video stimuli?
items.whatTheyDid: Gifford and colleagues collected 128-channel EEG and eye-tracking data from six participants viewing 1,102 three-second audiovisual clips under central-fixation instructions. The same stimuli are represented in an existing fMRI dataset.
items.whatTheyFound: The authors report time-linked neural responses and successful encoding of stimulus features. Raw and processed recordings, stimuli and metadata support reuse. The small participant sample and fixation constraint limit generalization to natural media consumption.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX can use the shared stimuli to test event-representation methods across EEG and fMRI datasets. Neural stimulus decoding is not a measure of individual belief, agreement or persuasion.
items.streamTitle: EEG Moments Dataset enables time-resolved study of audiovisual events
items.streamSummary: A public dataset pairs EEG and gaze from six participants with 1,102 short audiovisual clips, enabling time-resolved research on event perception.
items.attribution: Gifford, Oyarzo, Zonneveld et al. — Scientific Data (accepted data descriptor; November 27, 2026)
